feed.title: Lichen: L2s In CHannels ENforced on bitcoin

entry.title: Lichen: L2s In CHannels ENforced on bitcoin
entry.summary:
Recent updates have significantly improved the efficiency of onchain dispute resolution by substituting BABE for BitVMX. This modification lowers both the transaction count in a full dispute—from approximately 20-25 transactions to just 4 or 5—and the associated onchain cost, which now stands at around 30 kilobytes instead of 200. The EC scalar multiplication garbled circuit requires users to store 240MB, as detailed in [this note](https://github.com/AdamISZ/bitvmx/blob/master/docs/babe.md), but overall costs remain low. BABE integrates seamlessly with Lichen, enabling a streamlined prove-disprove process prior to contract signing and making large-scale mass exit scenarios more manageable. By mitigating mass exit risk, a single hub can now realistically support tens of thousands of users, in contrast to previous limitations that capped capacity at a few thousand. Liquidity requirements, particularly those akin to the "LSP" model, continue to serve as the primary bottleneck for scaling.
The latest version of the research paper, available [here](https://github.com/AdamISZ/bitvmx/blob/master/docs/paper.md), has been revised to emphasize the pure Lichen design. This approach utilizes a two-of-two contract structure enforced by a verification gadget, currently defaulting to BABE, though BitVMX remains an option within the codebase. A supplementary paper provides further technical details on the implementation of an L2 solution, including a sequencer, validity proofs, shielded notes, and finality anchored in Bitcoin. The implementation is complete but still rough in places; the subsidiary reference can be found [here](https://github.com/AdamISZ/bitvmx/blob/master/docs/subsidiary-paper.md).
The framework is adaptable and not limited to a particular L2 design. As long as state verification is possible, integration with various consensus models—such as signing quorums, proof of work, or proof of stake, potentially even using Ethereum smart contracts—is feasible. The chosen architecture validates state updates, establishes finality via Bitcoin postings, and entrusts the hub (as the sequencer) with bundling state changes. This setup necessitates a robust proof-counterproof mechanism to ensure secure exits, particularly when facing a malicious hub operator. More nuanced discussions of this are present in the referenced materials.
Further optimizations are under consideration, such as employing a "10 of 78 cut and choose" strategy—an idea recommended by both Glock and the original BABE paper—to reduce user storage requirements. Speculation exists that advances like Duty Free Bits could further decrease the 240MB storage overhead, although these improvements remain unconfirmed. Overall, the evolving design demonstrates strong potential for secure and scalable contract enforcement, even when the L2 operator behaves adversarially, with ongoing research focusing on issues such as data availability.
